title: AIRES Colombia 585
summary: AIRES Colombia Flight 585 crashed into a mountainside at 8,600 feet during approach to Cali. The crew was descending in poor visibility with mist and intermittent showers obscuring the ground. Weather conditions required instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) procedures, but the crew did not transition from visual flight rules, instead deviating from the assigned flight corridor and descending below safe altitude without visual references. The investigation found that the crew did not follow the flight path given by ground personnel and flew outside their assigned corridor.
probable_cause: The accident was caused by controlled flight into terrain resulting from the crew failing to follow assigned flight path procedures. The crew did not transition from VFR to IMC procedures when visibility deteriorated, flew outside the assigned flight corridor, and descended below safe altitude without maintaining visual reference to terrain. The poor visibility and mist prevented the crew from seeing the mountainside ahead.

factors.evidence: The aircraft crashed into the mountainside at an altitude of 8,600 feet while on approach to Cali, killing all 17 occupants.
The crew did not follow the flight path given by ground personnel and flew outside of the flight path, which increased the risk of veering off course.
Weather was poor with low visibility, mist and intermittent showers on the flight path, which obscured the ground and the terrain.
The crew continued descent below safe altitude when they did not have visual references to the terrain due to the mist and clouds.
The crew did not follow instrument landing conditions (IMC) procedures when required by weather conditions; they were required to switch from VFR to IMC but did not do so.

The aircraft burst into flames upon ground impact, killing 58 of 80 people on board.

summary: Iberia Flight 610, a Boeing 727 on a short domestic hop from Madrid to Bilbao, crashed into a ravine on Mount Oiz on 19 February 1985 after its left wing struck a television antenna during the approach in fog, killing all 141 passengers and 7 crew. Spanish investigators found the autopilot's altitude-select system had failed to engage, letting the aircraft descend past its target altitude, and that the crew misread the altitude alerts and kept descending during a turn that took them into the fog-shrouded mountain.

title: China Airlines 006
summary: A Boeing 747SP lost thrust in the No. 4 engine at 41,000 feet cruising over the Pacific. The flight engineer did not close the required bleed valve during the restart attempt, and as airspeed decreased, the autopilot reached maximum aileron trim while the aircraft began to roll. The captain disconnected the autopilot and recovered from a 31,500-foot dive with the aircraft experiencing g-forces as high as 5g. The diversion to San Francisco was completed safely but the aircraft sustained significant structural damage.
probable_cause: Over-reliance on the autopilot masked the approaching loss of airplane control, and the captain's distractions with engine restart and airspeed management prevented prompt recognition of the upset condition.

factors.evidence: The sequence began with a loss of thrust in the No. 4 engine.
The flight engineer attempted to restore power to the engine but did not close the bleed valve as required by the checklist procedure.
The captain over-relied on the autopilot and that this was also causal to the accident since the autopilot effectively masked the approaching onset of the loss of control of the airplane.
During this sequence of events, the aircraft was on autopilot, the airspeed slowly decreased.

The autopilot slowly applied more aileron to keep the wings level until the maximum limit of 23 degrees was reached. As the speed decreased further, the aircraft began to roll to the right even though the autopilot was maintaining maximum left roll input.

By the time the captain disconnected the autopilot the aircraft had rolled over and plunged 31500 ft, experiencing high speeds and g-forces as high as 5 g before the captain was able to recover from the dive.

events.text: Aircraft cruising at 41,000 feet, 350 miles northwest of San Francisco, when No. 4 engine lost thrust.
Flight engineer attempted to restore power but did not close the bleed valve as required by the checklist procedure.
Airspeed slowly decreased as aircraft remained on autopilot; autopilot applied more aileron to keep wings level until reaching maximum 23 degree limit.
Aircraft began to roll to the right despite maximum left roll input from autopilot; nose started to drop.
Captain disconnected the autopilot after aircraft had rolled over and begun plunging.
Captain recovered from the dive after experiencing g-forces as high as 5g and a 31,500-foot altitude loss.
Noting damage including bent wings, ripped horizontal stabilizer and lost elevator, captain diverted to San Francisco International Airport.

title: Japan Air Lines 123
summary: Japan Air Lines Flight 123 suffered explosive decompression 12 minutes after takeoff from Tokyo when an aft pressure bulkhead, repaired seven years earlier, finally failed, rupturing all four hydraulic systems and ejecting the vertical stabiliser. The crew flew under minimal control for 32 minutes before the Boeing 747 crashed near Mount Takamagahara, killing 520 of 524 aboard. The 1978 repair had used two splice plates instead of Boeing's specified continuous plate, cutting fatigue resistance to about 70 percent of a correct repair.
probable_cause: The aft pressure bulkhead, repaired after a 1978 tailstrike with two splice plates instead of Boeing's specified continuous plate, gradually cracked under pressurization cycles and failed after 12,318 flights, causing decompression that severed all hydraulic lines and left the aircraft uncontrollable.

events.text: During the 1978 tailstrike on landing at Osaka's Itami Airport, the pilot excessively flared the aircraft on a second touchdown, cracking open the aft pressure bulkhead.
Boeing technicians repaired the bulkhead with two splice plates instead of one continuous splice plate with three rows of rivets as required, and JAL's post-repair inspection missed the defect.
Twelve minutes after takeoff the faultily repaired bulkhead failed, causing decompression that ruptured all four hydraulic systems and ejected the vertical stabiliser.
With flight controls disabled the aircraft became uncontrollable, and the crew flew under minimal control for 32 minutes before the final crash.
In a 40-degree bank the right wing clipped a ridge near Mount Takamagahara, and the aircraft flipped over and struck another ridge before exploding.

title: Bar Harbor Airlines 1808
summary: Bar Harbor Airlines Flight 1808, a Beechcraft Model 99, departed Logan International Airport in Boston for Bangor, Maine, with planned stops in Augusta and Waterville, including an unscheduled flag stop in Auburn/Lewiston. At 22:00 EDT, weather at Auburn consisted of a 300-foot obscured indefinite ceiling, 1-mile visibility, and light drizzle. A Portland controller advised the flight it was drifting east of the ILS approach course and instructed a heading of 340 degrees. The aircraft flew through the approach course, requiring a 60-degree right turn less than 1 nautical mile from the outer marker. The aircraft did not begin descent until after passing Lewiston, already above the glide slope, causing the crew to rush the descent and approach with a steep descent profile. The aircraft crashed into trees 4,007 feet from the runway end and 440 feet to the right of centerline. All eight people on board were killed.
probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determined the accident was caused by the crew's continued attempt to stabilize an unstable approach rather than executing a missed approach. Contributing factors included a late and large course correction by the controller that the captain accepted, possible altimeter setting error, the crew descending below the applicable minimum descent altitude without the required visual references, and continued descent below the published glide slope during a night approach in low visibility.

title: Arrow Air 1285R
summary: Arrow Air Flight 1285R stalled and crashed shortly after takeoff from Gander, Newfoundland on December 12, 1985. The aircraft had accumulated ice contamination on the wings' leading edges during its earlier approach and refueling stop at Gander. The aircraft was not de-iced prior to takeoff, and the ice buildup degraded lift, resulting in a stall at low altitude from which recovery was not possible.
probable_cause: The most probable cause of the stall was ice contamination on the leading edge and upper surface of the wing following freezing precipitation exposure without de-icing before takeoff, combined with high drag and reduced lift conditions and possibly underestimated onboard weight.

factors.evidence: The aircraft stalled at low altitude from which recovery was not possible.
Ice contamination on the leading edge and upper surface of the wing resulted from precipitation conditions favorable for ice formation and freezing and frozen precipitation.
Prior to takeoff the aircraft had not been de-iced despite exposure to freezing and frozen precipitation.
Underestimated onboard weight may have compounded the effects of the contamination.
A non-functioning cockpit area microphone went undetected for an indeterminate number of flights, and no steps on standard checklists tested its functionality.
The defect in the cockpit area microphone went undetected due to no testing procedure on standard checklists.

events.text: During approach to Gander, precipitation conditions were favorable for formation of ice on wings.
After landing, aircraft remained exposed to freezing and frozen precipitation without de-icing.
Aircraft began takeoff roll on runway 22, rotated at 167 knots after 51 seconds, showing difficulty gaining altitude.
Airspeed reached 172 knots then decreased; aircraft descended after crossing Trans-Canada Highway 900 feet from runway departure end.
Aircraft struck terrain just short of Gander Lake approximately 3500 feet beyond runway departure end, broke up and exploded.
